newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich urges end to "tiresome" Republican turmoil.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich urges end to "tiresome" Republican turmoil.

text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich, still in charge of fractious Republicans, asked his colleagues on Wednesday to put to rest the "tiresome and overwrought saga" of plots against him and get back to work.

The Georgia Republican agreed to gather the party for a Wednesday night "family discussion" after his supporters and those in the dissident camp said their differences and a failed challenge to his leadership could not be swept under the rug.
He had opposed such a conference on Tuesday, saying the focus should immediately return to passage of the party's central goals -- cutting taxes and balancing the budget.

"I strongly encourage every Republican member to participate in this dialogue. Let me emphasise: I will not allow another chapter to be written in this tiresome and overwrought saga. This discussion will be the end of the story," he said as divided and anxious Republicans began a routine morning meeting to discuss upcoming legislation.

Republican unrest grew this year as the party returned from the 1996 elections with a narrowed majority in the House and less political leverage to use in talks with President Bill Clinton on crucial budget and tax issues.
This has proved particularly disturbing to a group of conservatives, many of whom were swept to power in 1994 when the party reclaimed its majority after 40 years.

Dissension within the ranks had to be quelled several times, but reached a fever pitch earlier this month when conservatives advocating a harder line in talks with the White House met to discuss ousting the speaker. Their effort was aborted and they never settled on a candidate to replace Gingrich.
The embattled speaker narrowly won re-election to his position in January and was reprimanded and fined by his colleagues for ethics violations.

Gingrich on Tuesday said there should be no retribution against any of his deputies who participated in the talks. One of his hand-picked emissaries to the rank-and-file, Representative Bill Paxon of New York, stepped down from his leadership post last week, saying he felt he no longer had the speaker's trust and confidence.
His chief deputy, Majority Leader Dick Armey of Texas, issued a statement on Tuesday denying he was involved in a plan to remove the speaker.

The dissidents said they believed they had encouragement from the leadership to go ahead with the plan and cited the role of party whip Tom DeLay. The Texas lawmaker has not issued a statement on his involvement other than to say he would not resign his post.
Trying to bring the focus back to work on taxes and the budget, Republican conference chairman John Boehner appeared before television cameras with the top tax and budget writers.

"Nobody knows what is going to happen tonight. Obviously there is going to be a lot of discussion. Hopefully, it will be very calm and everybody will be able to come together," House Budget Committee chairman John Kasich of Ohio said.

Both Kasich and Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer of Texas said the internal party turmoil had not had an impact on their negotiations on taxes or spending cuts. Republicans have reached a unified position on both issues and open face-to-face negotiations with administration officials later on Wednesday.
